planting.note: Divide and transplant rooted rhizome sections in early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil beneath conifers or oaks, since this dry-shade native resents heavy, poorly drained ground.

directions: Divide and transplant rooted rhizome sections in early spring into humus-rich, well-drained soil beneath conifers or oaks, since this dry-shade native resents heavy, poorly drained ground. Wiry black stems carry leathery, trifoliate leaflets year-round and send up airy sprays of small, nodding, golden-yellow flowers in late spring, giving the plant its common name for the way the petals appear to fold back. Unlike many woodland groundcovers, established plants tolerate the dry summer shade found under mature conifers along the West Coast and need little supplemental water once rooted in. It slowly forms a dense, weed-suppressing evergreen mat that pairs well with sword fern and other dry-shade natives.

planting.note: Set divisions of the shallow, creeping rhizome into consistently moist, humus-rich soil beneath a closed woodland canopy in early spring, spacing plants to allow the arching stems room to spread.

directions: Set divisions of the shallow, creeping rhizome into consistently moist, humus-rich soil beneath a closed woodland canopy in early spring, spacing plants to allow the arching stems room to spread. Paired lance-shaped leaves line each gently curving stem, and in mid-spring pairs of ivory, bell-shaped flowers dangle beneath the foliage before giving way to orange-red berries in late summer. Native to moist coastal forests from British Columbia to central California, it thrives in the same deep shade and leafy soil favored by ferns, wild ginger, and trillium. It spreads gradually into a loose colony but is never aggressive, making it a good textural companion in a naturalistic shade border.

planting.note: Plant divisions of the clumping rootstock in fall or early spring into rich, evenly moist soil in a lightly shaded bed, and top-dress with leaf mold to mimic its native forest floor.

directions: Plant divisions of the clumping rootstock in fall or early spring into rich, evenly moist soil in a lightly shaded bed, and top-dress with leaf mold to mimic its native forest floor. Slender, bamboo-like stems arch outward and carry glossy, pleated leaves, with clusters of soft yellow, pendant, tubular flowers dangling from the stem tips in mid-spring. Native to woodlands in China, Korea, and Japan, it forms a tidy, slowly expanding clump rather than running underground, so it stays well behaved among hostas, hellebores, and other shade perennials. Cut back the fading foliage in autumn to keep the planting tidy through winter.

planting.note: Transplant rooted runners in early spring into cool, acidic, humus-rich soil with sharp drainage, ideally on a shaded slope or among rocks where water never stands.

directions: Transplant rooted runners in early spring into cool, acidic, humus-rich soil with sharp drainage, ideally on a shaded slope or among rocks where water never stands. Rounded, glossy, scalloped leaves take on bronze and red tones through winter, and in early spring wiry stems lift dainty, nodding, deeply fringed bells in shades of pink or white. This Japanese woodland native spreads slowly by creeping stems to form a low mat and is prized in shaded rock gardens for its combination of year-round foliage color and delicate spring flowers. It performs best where summers stay cool and moist, and it resists heavy clay or soil that dries out completely.

planting.note: Move small divisions along with a generous scoop of their native soil into acidic, humus-rich ground beneath pines or mixed hardwoods, disturbing the root zone as little as possible to protect the fungal partners the plant depends on.

directions: Move small divisions along with a generous scoop of their native soil into acidic, humus-rich ground beneath pines or mixed hardwoods, disturbing the root zone as little as possible to protect the fungal partners the plant depends on. Its low rosette of dark green leaves is netted with fine silvery-white veining and stays attractive through winter, while a slender spike of small, white, hooded flowers appears in summer. Because it relies on an intact mycorrhizal relationship, this native orchid rarely thrives if transplanted into ordinary garden soil, so it is best grown as a foliage accent in an undisturbed woodland setting rather than a typical perennial bed. Its patterned leaves make it a subtle but rewarding groundcover for collectors of native shade flora.

planting.note: Move divisions with an intact clump of surrounding native soil into cool, consistently moist, humus-rich woodland ground, disturbing the roots as little as possible since this species partially depends on mycorrhizal fungi in undisturbed forest soil.

directions: Move divisions with an intact clump of surrounding native soil into cool, consistently moist, humus-rich woodland ground, disturbing the roots as little as possible since this species partially depends on mycorrhizal fungi in undisturbed forest soil. Rounded, leathery, evergreen leaves form a low basal rosette, and a short raceme of small, pale pink, cup-shaped flowers nods above the foliage in mid to late summer. Found in cool coniferous and mixed forests across much of the Northern Hemisphere, it is better suited to being preserved in a naturally wooded corner of the garden than transplanted into a conventional perennial border. Its neat, ground-hugging rosettes offer a subtle, textural note among mosses and other diminutive woodland plants.

planting.note: Move small clumps with generous surrounding native soil into cool, moist, acidic humus in deep conifer shade, taking care not to break up the fine root system that ties this plant to its fungal partners.

directions: Move small clumps with generous surrounding native soil into cool, moist, acidic humus in deep conifer shade, taking care not to break up the fine root system that ties this plant to its fungal partners. Each slender stem bears a single loose rosette of small rounded leaves and lifts one nodding, waxy-white, sweetly fragrant flower with a prominent green style in early to midsummer. It is among the most difficult native wildflowers to establish outside its natural forest floor, so gardeners are best served by protecting existing colonies rather than attempting to relocate them into cultivated beds. Where it does persist, its solitary, jewel-like blossom makes it one of the most charming finds on a shaded woodland walk.

planting.note: Divide the fleshy-rooted clumps in early spring or fall and replant into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in a cool, lightly shaded spot, keeping the crown just below the soil surface.

directions: Divide the fleshy-rooted clumps in early spring or fall and replant into rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in a cool, lightly shaded spot, keeping the crown just below the soil surface. Loose racemes of vivid, true-blue, tubular flowers rise above finely divided, blue-green foliage from mid-spring into early summer, offering one of the purest blue tones available among shade perennials. The plant tends to go semi-dormant in hot, humid weather, so it performs best where summers stay relatively cool and the soil never dries out completely. Pair it with hostas, ferns, or other later-emerging perennials that can fill in as it fades back after flowering.

planting.note: Divide established clumps in spring and set the divisions into cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in dappled or full shade.

directions: Divide established clumps in spring and set the divisions into cool, humus-rich, evenly moist soil in dappled or full shade. Finely dissected, fern-like foliage emerges bronze-purple in cool spring weather and gradually mellows toward green as temperatures rise, while loose clusters of small pink to lavender flowers appear above the leaves in spring. Its low, mounding habit and colorful new growth make it a useful edging or front-of-border plant in a shaded woodland bed, especially paired with contrasting gold or chartreuse foliage nearby. Like many Corydalis species it prefers consistent moisture and cool summers, and it can decline in prolonged heat and humidity.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)

common_name: Night Heron Fairy Bells (Black-Stemmed Canton Fairybells)

planting.note: Plant divisions of the clumping rhizome in spring into rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered, shaded bed, mulching to protect the crown through winter at the cooler end of its range.

directions: Plant divisions of the clumping rhizome in spring into rich, well-drained soil in a sheltered, shaded bed, mulching to protect the crown through winter at the cooler end of its range. Tall, cane-like stems emerge near-black and arch upward, clothed in glossy, dark green, lance-shaped leaves, with small creamy bell-shaped flowers dangling from the leaf axils in spring and dark berries following in fall. The striking near-black stems give this selection a bold, almost bamboo-like presence that stands out among hostas, ferns, and other shade perennials. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than the wild species, so gardeners at the cold end of its range should give it a protected spot and a heavy winter mulch.

common_name: Cameo Rue Anemone (Double Pink Rue Anemone)

planting.note: Plant small tuberous divisions in fall into humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil, setting them a couple of inches deep among leaf litter beneath deciduous trees.

directions: Plant small tuberous divisions in fall into humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil, setting them a couple of inches deep among leaf litter beneath deciduous trees. This selection produces fully double, powder-pink, pompon-like flowers held just above delicate, blue-green foliage divided into rounded leaflets reminiscent of meadow rue. Like the wild species it is an ephemeral that goes dormant by midsummer, so it pairs well with later-emerging ferns or hostas that can fill the space it leaves behind. A long-lived, slow-spreading choice for a shaded rock garden or woodland edge, it rewards patience with an increasingly showy display each spring.
